Keywords: Whatever, Attracts, And

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering that preserves the original meaning while enhancing its clarity and elegance:

---

Whatever thou art, whose beauty here below
So draws thee that thou stream and flow,
And wind and curl, and wink and smile,
Still shifting both thy course and guile;
Though thy close commerce nothing bars
My present search—for eagles heed not stars,
And ever is the lesser blest
By that which is the highest and the best—
Yet, seeing all that lives and doth subsist
Receives its warrant from divinity,
And teaches us our duty, I would see
What man may learn from thee.

First, I am sure, the subject thus respected
Is nobly framed; for bodies once infected,
Depraved, or dead, can share with thee
No hold, nor any sympathy.
Next, there resides a restless, pure desire,
A longing for thy bright and vital fire—
Desire that never shall be quenched,
Nor ever writhed away, nor wrenched.

These are the magnets that so strongly move
And work all night upon thy light and love,
As forms of beauty, though we know not why,
Command and gently guide the eye.
For where desire—celestial, pure desire—
Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire,
There God ordains a commerce, and He sheds
His secret grace upon their heads.

This is the heart He craves; and whosoever will
But give it Him, and grudge it not, shall feel
That God is true, as herbs unseen
Put forth their youth and living green.

---

Would you like me to adopt a particular tone (more archaic, more modern, or more formal still), or adjust the meter and rhyme more strictly?
outputs.L2:
Whatever you may be—you whose loveliness in this earthly realm draws me so, causing you to pour forth and glide, to twist and spiral, to twinkle and grin, changing your motion and your cunning tricks—although your intimate exchange in no way blocks my current inquiry (for eagles do not gaze at stars, and always the humbler thing is blessed by the finest and the greatest good); still, since everything that lives and exists holds its authority from the divine and instructs us in our obligations, I intend to discover what a person might gain from you.

To begin, I feel certain that whatever object receives such favor is well arranged, for things that are once tainted, corrupted, or lifeless can share no bond or connection with you.

Furthermore, within it dwells a tireless, unmixed yearning and craving for your radiant, life-giving flame—a longing that can never be extinguished, nor twisted away, nor forced apart.

These are the forces that pull so powerfully and labor throughout the night upon your radiance and affection, just as lovely forms, for reasons unknown to us, direct and steer our sight.

For wherever longing—heavenly, unmixed longing—has settled in, and flourishes, and does not weary, there God establishes an exchange and pours his hidden gift upon them.

This is the heart he longs for, and whoever is willing to surrender it to him without resentment will come to know that God holds true, just as unseen plants clothe themselves in fresh green youth.
outputs.L3:
**Lessons Drawn from a Natural Marvel**

The speaker stands in quiet observation before a natural phenomenon whose beauty is never still. It moves, it shifts, it flickers and reshapes itself before his eyes, and in its restless play he finds something more than idle wonder. He resolves, therefore, to study it closely—not merely to admire, but to learn. For if nature offers such a spectacle, surely it must carry within it some instruction, some lesson that humanity might gather and carry away for its own betterment.

As he reflects, he arrives at a first conclusion: whatever it is that draws this beauty toward itself must be, by its very nature, well-disposed and wholesome. For beauty of this kind will not consort with what is corrupt. Depraved, decaying, or lifeless bodies hold no sympathy with it and can form no bond with its brightness. The connection it seeks is with what is pure and alive; there is a kind of moral selectivity in its movement, a refusal to attach itself to anything tainted or dead.

Within the phenomenon, the speaker perceives a restless and unclouded desire—a longing that never rests and never fades. It reaches always toward what is bright and full of life, yearning for a vital fire that cannot be seized by force. One cannot wrench this longing away or bend it to another purpose; it belongs entirely to itself, moving according to its own pure inclination.

This desire, he observes, behaves like a magnet. It does not command by violence but draws all things toward it naturally, effortlessly, as though by an inner law. Just as a beautiful form, without speaking a word, instinctively captures and commands the eye that beholds it, so this pure longing guides and gathers what belongs to it, exercising a quiet authority that needs no compulsion.

And here the speaker reaches his final and highest thought. Wherever such a celestial and unspoiled desire takes root and is allowed to grow, God Himself enters into the matter. He establishes a bond, forms a covenant with those who remain faithful, and rewards their steadfastness. His truth is thereby proven—made visible not through argument but through life itself—just as hidden herbs, unseen beneath the soil, at last break forth and bloom green with the freshness of youth. In this way, the invisible faithfulness of God is confirmed by the visible flourishing of what is pure.
outputs.L4:
# The Star's Sacred Teaching

Gazing upward at the radiant star suspended in the night sky, we might well ask ourselves: what wisdom does such celestial beauty hold for us mortals below? The star burns with a brilliance that seems to speak of something beyond mere astronomy—a language of the spirit written in light across the heavens. In its steady glow, we perceive not just a distant flame but a teacher offering lessons to the attentive soul.

Consider how the star seems drawn toward that which is pure and rightly ordered. Just as light finds its truest reflection in clear and unclouded surfaces, so too does the star's radiance appear to seek out subjects that are clean of heart and well-disposed toward goodness. This natural attraction becomes for us a living metaphor—an image of divine communion itself. For does not God, like this luminous body, incline toward the soul that has prepared itself, that has made itself receptive and worthy through purity of intention?

Herein lies the poem's deeper revelation. Where such celestial desire takes root—where the longing for heavenly things germinates within the human breast—there God establishes a sacred commerce with the soul. This is no ordinary transaction but a holy exchange, an intimate trade between the divine and the human, wherein grace flows toward the heart that has opened itself to receive.

The speaker arrives at a profound conclusion: those who freely and willingly offer their hearts to God will come to know His faithfulness in the most intimate way. This faithfulness works not through spectacle or force but through quiet, natural renewal—like unseen herbs that, hidden beneath the soil, silently restore and refresh the vitality of all that grows. So does God's constancy work within the surrendered soul, unseen yet ever-present, replenishing the spirit with a life that never fails. The lesson of the star, then, is ultimately this: give yourself freely, and you shall be renewed beyond all measure.
outputs.L5:
# Whatever You Focus On, Attracts More of the Same

There is an old idea that has echoed through philosophy, psychology, and everyday wisdom for centuries: whatever we give our attention to tends to grow. This simple principle carries a surprising amount of weight when we examine how we move through our lives.

**Whatever** we choose to dwell on shapes our reality more than we often realize. If we spend our days replaying frustrations, worrying about what could go wrong, or comparing ourselves to others, those thoughts begin to color everything we see. On the other hand, when we direct our minds toward gratitude, opportunity, and growth, we start noticing possibilities we might have missed before. The word "whatever" is powerful precisely because it is so open-ended—it reminds us that the choice of focus is ultimately ours.

This is where the idea of what **attracts** us becomes important. Our energy, mood, and mindset act almost like a magnet. A person who radiates optimism and openness naturally draws others toward them, while someone caught in negativity often finds that their outlook keeps that negativity close. This isn't magic; it's a reflection of how attention, behavior, and consequence are linked. What we cultivate inside tends to be what we attract from the world around us.

**And** perhaps that is the most important lesson of all: our inner world and our outer experiences are deeply connected. The thoughts we nurture, the attitudes we hold, and the intentions we set all combine to influence the direction our lives take. Change begins not by controlling everything outside of us, but by choosing what we allow to occupy our minds.

So the next time you catch yourself dwelling on something, pause and ask: is this what I want more of? Because whatever you focus on grows, whatever you emphasize attracts, and the balance between them shapes the life you build.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphysical poem in the style of Henry Vaughan addressed to something in nature, exploring how it teaches spiritual lessons about God and the soul's desire.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Streamlet's Sermon

Thou restless silver in the vale below,
 That never sleeps nor stays,
How dost thou teach my sluggish soul to flow
 And spend itself in praise!

For thou wert born within some secret hill,
 A hidden mother-spring,
And thence, obedient to thy Maker's will,
 Dost run and run, and sing.

Thou seek'st the sea though thou hast never seen
 That great unbounded main;
Yet by an instinct pure, an inward mean,
 Thou hurriest to that plain.

So should my spirit, exiled here in clay,
 Feel homeward-drawing tides,
And know its ocean though so far away,
 Where its true Rest abides.

Thou tak'st no thought to hoard thy passing store,
 But givest all thou art;
The more thou losest, thou art rich the more—
 O emblem for my heart!

For I have grasped, and grasping, held but sand,
 While thou, by pouring, live;
Teach me this alchemy I understand
 Too little: how to give.

When rocks obstruct, thou dost not stay to fight,
 But round them, murmuring, wind;
And leav'st thy quarrel to the patient right
 Of Him who all designed.

Yet in thy depth, where all the sky is met,
 I read a stranger thing:
Thou bear'st Heaven's image on thy surface, wet
 And trembling, like a wing.

So may my troubled glass, when it lies still,
 Some borrowed brightness keep,
And show, poor mirror on this darkened hill,
 The Sun I cannot reap.

Run on, sweet preacher; when thy course is done
 And thou art lost in sea,
Thou art not lost, but gathered into One—
 As I would gather'd be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a 17th-century devotional poem where the speaker contemplates an object of natural beauty and reflects on divine love and pure desire.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon a Rose at Morning**

Fair blushing thing, that on the briar dost stand,
Wrought in a night by no man's careful art,
I take thee gently in my trembling hand
And read a sermon writ upon my heart:
    For who but Love could such a colour lay,
    And fold this crimson from the common clay?

Thou wear'st thy beauty as a borrowed dress,
Lent for a morning, gathered by the noon;
Thy sweetness is a kind of holiness
That preaches unto men, *I perish soon*—
    Yet in thy dying I am taught to see
    A fairer bloom that shall not fade in me.

I will not love thee as the wanton eye
That plucks the flower and lets the giver go,
But climb by thee, as by a ladder, high,
Past all the pretty things He plants below;
    For every grace that in thy leaves I find
    Is but a whisper of a greater Mind.

Then let desire be pure, and mount above,
Refined by looking on so frail a fire;
Teach me, O Rose, to turn my earthward love
Into a clean and heaven-seeking desire—
    That when thy petals to the dust are cast,
    My longing, purged, may hold its Lord at last.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem imitating the 1600s religious verse tradition, using archaic language like "'tis" and "nought," about how earthly beauty points toward heavenly truth?
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon the Rose, a Meditation**

'Tis not the flower alone I do adore,
When morning gilds the garden with her light;
Each petal is a glass, and nothing more,
Wherein I glimpse a fairer, purer sight.

For earthly beauty, be it ne'er so sweet,
Is but a borrowed lustre from Above;
The rose that blushes crimson at my feet
Doth wear the livery of its Maker's love.

Nought here below can perfect grace impart,
Yet all things whisper of a higher throne:
The lily's white, the wren's untutored art,
Are letters spelling what is His alone.

So when I gaze upon a comely face,
Or hear the brook go singing to the sea,
'Tis but a shadow cast by heav'nly Grace,
A finger pointing where I ought to be.

Then let me love the creature, but not stay,
Nor mire my soul in dust that soon must fall;
For Beauty is a candle, and the day
It doth foretell shall one day swallow all.

Lord, teach mine eye to look, and looking, climb—
From flower to Thee, from moment unto ever;
That I, who dwell in these poor courts of time,
May trace Thy Beauty home, and lose it never.

---

I leaned on the devotional style of poets like George Herbert and Henry Vaughan—the emblematic reading of nature as a "glass" or book, the turn from creature to Creator, and the plain-yet-elevated diction. Happy to adjust the tone, add stanzas, or lean more toward Donne's knottier metaphysical manner if you'd like.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem addressed to a mysterious natural phenomenon that streams, flows, and curls, drawing moral and religious meaning from observing it.
counterfactuals.output:
# To the Aurora

O silent fire that walks the northern night,
What hand unrolls your banner in the dark?
You stream in ribbons of unearthly light,
And curl like breath above the world's cold arc.

I watch you flow where no still thing remains—
Green rivers spilling down the vault of stars,
You bend and braid in luminous refrains,
Then part like veils across the heaven's bars.

No engine drives you, yet you never rest;
No painter mixed the colors that you wear.
What law compels you, curling east to west,
To dance unseen by half the sleeping air?

And here I learn the lesson of the sky:
That beauty asks no audience to be shown.
You would have streamed though no one passed you by—
You praise your Maker faithful and alone.

So let my small devotions imitate
Your quiet flame that flickers unadmired;
Let me not seek the crowd, the loud, the great,
But burn because the burning is required.

For if the light obeys a hidden call
And curls its glory through the empty height,
Then surely He who set it there sees all—
And loves the soul that shines, though hid from sight.

Teach me to flow as you have learned to flow,
To bend and yield yet never quite depart,
To trust the wind whose reasons I can't know,
And hold the sacred silence in my heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphysical religious poem with short-and-long line stanzas about how desire for God's light dwells in a pure heart.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Lamp Within**

Cleanse thou the glass,
And light will find its lodging there;
No stain of pride, no dust of self may pass
The threshold of that inmost air
Where longing, like a flame,
Leans upward to its Name.

For God is light,
And light will only rest and dwell
In chambers swept of shadow and of night,
As water seeks the deepest well;
The pure alone can hold
That undiminished gold.

Desire is deep—
It burrows where the soul is cleft,
And in the wound it makes, it learns to keep
A hunger nothing else has left;
Thus emptiness is grace,
A hollow made for space.

O paradox:
The heart most bare is filled the most,
And He who all our striving seals and locks
Is nearest to the humblest ghost;
The vessel scoured and thinned
Becomes His dwelling, wind

To catch His breath,
And mirror to reflect His fire.
Here in the little death of every death
The soul ignites its whole desire,
And finds, past every dim
Reflection, only Him.

So make me clear,
A pane through which Thy morning streams;
Take out the flaw, the fear, the wanting-here,
And leave the wanting that redeems—
That in my cleanness, Lord,
Thy light may be its own reward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
